findings.claim: For a 4-mark Describe, give four separate points rather than expanding one point at length.
findings.truth: This contradicts the lesson's own practice question 4, which asks for two differences and awards 2 marks per difference. On that question four bare statements would score at most 2 marks. The advice should be to make two points and develop each one.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 1 practice_questions[3] mark scheme ('[2 marks per difference]'); spec assessment section (five questions, one per topic, short- to extended-response items)

findings.claim: Layer-to-protocol mapping is examined almost every year and is worth 4–6 marks.
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about past papers. The spec states only that Paper 1 has five questions, one per topic, out of 75 marks, using multiple-choice, short-, medium- and extended-open-response, tabular and diagrammatic items. It says nothing about how often a sub-topic appears or what it is worth. First assessment was 2022, so 'almost every year' is also unsupportable.
findings.evidence: spec 'Assessment information' for Paper 1 (1CP2/01): five questions, one per topic, 75 marks, first assessment May/June 2022

findings.claim: Highly scalable for high-reliability environments such as core internet infrastructure, hospital networks or military communications.
findings.truth: Mesh is listed as an advantage of scalability, but a full mesh scales badly: connections grow as n(n-1)/2, so each new device needs a link to every existing device. The lesson's own disadvantage list says exactly this (45 links for 10 devices; 190 for 20). A student who writes 'mesh is highly scalable' would lose marks. The true advantage here is suitability for high-reliability settings, not scalability.
findings.evidence: recomputation of n(n-1)/2 (10 devices = 45, 20 devices = 190, both stated correctly elsewhere in the lesson); internal contradiction with lesson 3 disadvantage list

findings.claim: requires a valid SSL/TLS certificate which has a cost and must be renewed (mark scheme for the 6-mark HTTPS question)
findings.truth: Certificates are now routinely free (for example Let's Encrypt), so cost is no longer a general disadvantage of HTTPS; renewal is still true. Certificates are not named in the spec, so this sits outside assessed content and no student would be marked down either way. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: spec 4.1.6 names HTTP and HTTPS only; no certificate content in Topic 4

findings.claim: router are the signposts of the internet.
findings.truth: A number-agreement slip: the sentence starts with a singular noun and a plural verb. The same generator artefact appears in lesson 2 ('This works because of network protocol - agreed sets of rules'). Both are grammatical, not factual, and fixing them would mean editing the text inside a <dfn> element that the glossary keys on, so no edit is written.
findings.evidence: reading of lesson 1 content_html n15 and lesson 2 content_html n2

summary: Technically a strong unit: the four TCP/IP layers and their protocol mapping, TCP vs IP roles, MAC-at-Link vs IP-at-Internet, the topology properties, both transmission-time calculations (25 MiB at 100 Mbit/s = 2.097 s; 400 MiB at 80 Mbit/s = 41.94 s), every n(n-1)/2 mesh count and all 20 knowledge-check answer keys are correct, and scope matches spec 4.1.1-4.1.8 and 4.2.1 exactly with no Caesar cipher, UDP or encryption content imported from other boards or topics. The three fixes are all exam-guidance defects: one piece of advice that contradicts the lesson's own mark scheme, one fabricated claim about how often a sub-topic is examined and for how many marks, and one wrongly-labelled mesh advantage.
